::: {#sol-dot-variance}

Since $q_j$ and $k_j$ are independent,
each term $q_j k_j$ has mean $\E{q_j k_j} = \E{q_j} \E{k_j} = 0$.
Its variance is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Var{q_j k_j}
&= \E{q_j^2 k_j^2} - \paren{\E{q_j k_j}}^2 \\
&= \E{q_j^2} \E{k_j^2} - 0 && \text{(independence)} \\
&= 1 \cdot 1 && \text{(mean 0 and variance 1)} \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The $d_k$ terms are independent,
so their variances add:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Var{\dprod{\vq}{\vecf{k}}}
&= \Var{\sumto{j}{d_k} q_j k_j} \\
&= \sumto{j}{d_k} \Var{q_j k_j} && \text{(independent terms)} \\
&= d_k. && \text{(each variance is 1)}
\end{aligned}
$$

@vaswani2017attention [section 3.2.1, footnote 4] give the same argument.

```{python}
#| code-fold: show
generator = torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)
dims = [4, 64, 1024]
dot_vars = []
for d in dims:
    q_draws = torch.randn(10_000, d, generator=generator)
    k_draws = torch.randn(10_000, d, generator=generator)
    dot_vars.append((q_draws * k_draws).sum(dim=1).var().item())
print(dot_vars)
```

The variance grows in proportion to $d_k$.
From 10,000 draws,
the sample variances for $d_k = 4$, 64 and 1024 are
`r sprintf("%.1f", py$dot_vars[[1]])`,
`r sprintf("%.1f", py$dot_vars[[2]])` and
`r sprintf("%.0f", py$dot_vars[[3]])`.
Dividing a quantity by a constant $c$ divides its variance by $c^2$,
so dividing the [dot product](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/linear-algebra-vectors.html#def-dot-product) by $\sqrt{d_k}$ gives variance $d_k / d_k = 1$,
whatever $d_k$ is.

:::
